knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%",

  ggplot2.continuous.colour = "viridis",
  ggplot2.continuous.fill = "viridis"

scale_colour_discrete = scale_colour_viridis_d

## Problem 1
The `ny_noaa` dataset contains daily weather observations from New York State 
weather stations. It has `r format(nrow(ny_noaa), big.mark = ",")` rows 
and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables, covering `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` stations 
from `r min(ny_noaa$date)` to `r max(ny_noaa$date)`. 
The key variables are the station ID (`id`), the date (`date`), 
precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), 
and the maximum and minimum temperature (`tmax`, `tmin`).

### Data cleaning 
```{r}
ny_noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
```
I created separate variables for year, month, and day from `date`. 
The raw `tmax`, `tmin`, and `prcp` values are recorded in tenths of 
a unit (and `tmax` and `tmin` are stored as text), so I converted them 
to numbers and divided by 10 to obtain degrees Celsius and millimeters. 
Snowfall (`snow`) is already in millimeters. Some snowfall values are not 
physically plausible: `snow` ranges from `r min(ny_noaa$snow, na.rm = TRUE)` 
to `r max(ny_noaa$snow, na.rm = TRUE)` mm, 
and `r sum(ny_noaa$snow < 0, na.rm = TRUE)` values are negative. 
I kept them in the cleaned data; the snowfall plot below only uses values
between 0 and 100 mm.


### Missing data
```{r}
ny_noaa_clean |>
  summarize(
    across(c(prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, tmin), ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Percentage of missing values")
```
Missing data are a substantial issue: 43.7% of `tmax` and `tmin`, 
22.8% of `snwd`, 14.7% of `snow`, and 5.6% of `prcp` are missing, 
so temperature is the least complete variable.



### Snowfall values
```{r}

ny_noaa_clean |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Ten most common snowfall values (mm)")
```
The most common snowfall value is 0 mm (2,008,508 observations), 
accounting for about 77% of all observations and about 91% of observations 
with a recorded value. This is expected because it snows on only a small 
fraction of days, and almost never outside the winter months.

The second most common value is NA (381,221 observations), 
which means no measurement was recorded on those days. 
This is not the same as a day with no snowfall.

Among the non-zero values, the most frequent are 25, 13, 51 and 76 mm, 
which correspond closely to 1, 0.5, 2 and 3 inches (1 inch = 25.4 mm). 
This suggests that snowfall was originally recorded in inches 
and then converted to millimeters, so values near whole or half inches 
appear far more often than others.


### January and July mean maximum temperature
```{r}
monthly_tmax_df <-
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")


monthly_tmax_df |> summarize(n_nan = sum(is.nan(mean_tmax)), n_total = n())
```


### January and July mean maximum temperature
```{r}
monthly_tmax_df =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

```

```{r}
monthly_tmax_df |>
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c(1, 7), labels = c("January", "July"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .1) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1985, 1995, 2005)) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean maximum temperature by station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean maximum temperature (°C)"
  )

```
Station-year-months with no valid maximum temperature
(`r sum(is.nan(monthly_tmax_df$mean_tmax))` of `r nrow(monthly_tmax_df)`) are 
omitted from the plot.



To investigate the lowest July value, 
I looked at that station and year in more detail.
```{r}
monthly_tmax_df |>
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
  filter(
    (month == 7 & mean_tmax < 17) |
      (month == 1 & mean_tmax < -11)
  )

monthly_tmax_df |>
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
  filter(month == 7, mean_tmax < 17)

ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(id == "USC00308962", year == 1988, month == 7) |>
  summarize(n_days = n(), n_valid_tmax = sum(!is.na(tmax)))


ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(
    (id == "USC00301723" & year == 1982 & month == 1) |
      (id == "USC00305925" & year == 2005 & month == 1)
  ) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(n_days = n(), n_valid_tmax = sum(!is.na(tmax)), .groups = "drop")

```
The plot shows the mean maximum temperature for each station in January and July 
from 1981 to 2010; station-year-months with no valid 
`tmax` (`r sum(is.nan(monthly_tmax_df$mean_tmax))` of `r nrow(monthly_tmax_df)`) are omitted. 
In January, most station means range from about −10 to 8 °C, 
while in July they range from about 21 to 32 °C. The lines rise and fall together 
across stations, which suggests that year-to-year changes are at least partly driven 
by regional weather shared across stations rather than by local conditions, 
and this variation is larger in January than in July. I do not see a clear long-term 
increase or decrease over the 30 years. Three station-year-months stand out as outliers. 
Station USC00301723 in January 1982 has a mean of −13.4 °C, and station USC00308962 
in July 1988 has a mean of about 14 °C, far below the other stations that year; 
both are based on valid data for all 31 days, so they are unlikely to 
result from missing data and may reflect genuine cold spells or local measurement 
or recording problems, although this cannot be confirmed from these data alone. 
The third, station USC00305925 in January 2005 (−12.2 °C), is based on only 
1 valid day out of 31, so it reflects a single observation rather than a monthly 
average and should be interpreted cautiously.


### Temperature and snowfall plots
```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.asp = .5}
hex_plot =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  scale_fill_continuous(breaks = c(10000, 30000, 50000)) +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm")) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs minimum temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )

ridge_plot =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges() +
  scale_y_discrete(breaks = as.character(seq(1985, 2010, by = 5))) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall distribution by year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  )

hex_plot + ridge_plot
```
The left panel shows the relationship between daily minimum 
and maximum temperature for all observations. 
A hex plot is used because there are more than two million rows, 
and a scatterplot would be heavily overplotted.
About 44% of the rows have a missing tmax or 
tmin and are not shown in the left panel.
The two variables are positively associated: 
most observations fall in a narrow diagonal band, and the densest 
hexagons (more than 40,000 observations each) are around a minimum of 10–15 °C 
and a maximum of 20–25 °C. A few isolated hexagons are implausible, including 
maximum temperatures above 50 °C (some near 60 °C) and several points 
where the minimum temperature is higher than the maximum, such as 
a minimum near 50 °C with a maximum near 0 °C. These are likely recording errors.


```{r}
ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(tmin > tmax) |>
  count()

```
The right panel shows the distribution of snowfall values between 0 and 100 mm for each year. 
The distributions are similar across years: each has a large mass of small values 
(below about 15 mm), followed by smaller peaks near 25, 51 and 76 mm, 
which is consistent with snowfall being recorded in inches and then converted to millimeters. 
Differences between years are small. 
1183 observations have a minimum temperature higher than the maximum.



## Problem 2
### Load, tidy, and merge the data
```{r}
covar_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4, na = c("", ".", "NA")) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

accel_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_df =
  left_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn") |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("male", "female")),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

```
The covariate file has `r nrow(covar_df)` participants. 
After excluding those younger than 21 or with missing demographic data, 
`r nrow(nhanes_df)` participants remain (`r nrow(covar_df) - nrow(nhanes_df)` excluded). 
The final dataset keeps all originally observed variables; `sex` 
and `education` are coded as factors, with education ordered from lowest to highest.



### Education and sex
```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Number of men and women in each education category")

```
The table shows the number of men and women in each education category 
among the 228 participants aged 21 or older. 
The largest category is “More than high school” (n = 115). 
Men and women are similarly represented in “Less than high school” (27 vs. 28) 
and “More than high school” (56 vs. 59). The exception is “High school equivalent”, 
which has 35 men but only 23 women.



### Age distribution
```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution by education and sex",
    x = "Education",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  )

nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    median_age = median(age),
    q1_age = quantile(age, 0.25),
    q3_age = quantile(age, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Age summary by education and sex")

```
The boxplot shows that median age is 60 (men) and 61 (women) among participants 
with less than a high school education, compared with 43.5 (men) and 41 (women) 
among those with more than a high school education, 
suggesting that participants with more education tend to be younger. 
In the “High school equivalent” category, women are older than men (median 62 vs. 53), 
while sex differences are small in the other categories. 
However, the age distributions are wide and overlap substantially. 
For example, the middle 50% of women with a high school equivalent education range 
from 44.5 to 74.5 years.


### Total activity by age
To compare total activity, 
I converted the data to long format and summed the MIMS values 
over the 1,440 minutes of the day for each participant.
```{r}
nhanes_long =
  nhanes_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute_label",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(minute = parse_number(minute_label))

total_activity_df =
  nhanes_long |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims), .groups = "drop")

```



Next, I plotted total activity against age, 
using color for sex and a separate panel for each education level.
```{r, fig.width = 8}
total_activity_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
The scatterplot shows that total daily activity generally declines with age, 
but the pattern differs by education level. 
Among participants with less than a high school education, total activity falls 
from about 17,000–18,500 MIMS in the youngest participants to about 9,000 at age 80; 
women decline steadily, whereas men show a small rise around age 60 before dropping. 
In the high school equivalent group, women peak at about age 40 (roughly 17,000 MIMS), 
well above men (roughly 14,000), and both sexes level off at about 10,000 after age 60. 
In the more than high school group, the trends are flatter, 
and women have higher total activity than men at most ages. 
One man in this group (age 36) has a total activity of only 301 MIMS, 
which may reflect a device-wear or data issue worth checking. 
Because each panel contains relatively few participants and the points 
are widely scattered, the smooth curves should be interpreted as rough trends only.



### 24-hour activity profile
```{r}
activity_by_minute_df =
  nhanes_long |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(mean_mims = mean(mims), .groups = "drop")


activity_by_minute_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute / 60, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24)) +
  labs(
    title = "24-hour activity profile by education and sex",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Mean MIMS per minute",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
In all three education groups, activity is lowest in the early morning (around 3–5 AM), 
rises sharply between about 6 and 9 AM, remains high throughout the day, 
and declines in the evening. Among participants with less than a high school education, 
the profile peaks around midday at about 15 MIMS; men and women are nearly identical 
during the day, but men are more active than women overnight and in the early morning. 
In the high school equivalent group, women are slightly more active than men 
during the day (roughly 13 vs. 12 MIMS). The difference is largest in the more than 
high school group, where women remain at about 14 MIMS from late morning through 
the evening, while men show a dip in the mid-afternoon and a smaller second rise 
around 6 PM.Participants with a high school equivalent education have the lowest daytime 
activity of the three groups (about 12–13 MIMS, compared with about 14–15 in the 
other two groups).Overnight activity is low in all three education groups.
These curves show group averages at each minute and hide substantial individual 
variation. Education groups also differ in age (shown in the earlier boxplot), 
and total activity declines with age, so differences across education groups may 
partly reflect age rather than education itself.



## Problem 3
### Import and describe the data
```{r}
jan_2020_df <-
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "January")

jul_2020_df <-
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "July")

jan_2024_df <-
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "January")

jul_2024_df <-
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")

citi_df =
  bind_rows(jan_2020_df, jul_2020_df, jan_2024_df, jul_2024_df) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual)
  )

```
The Citi Bike dataset contains `r format(nrow(citi_df), big.mark = ",")` rides, 
drawn from a 1% sample of rides lasting less than 4 hours in each of four months: 
January and July of 2020 and 2024. There are `r ncol(citi_df)` variables: ride ID, 
bike type (`rideable_type`), day of the week (`weekdays`), 
ride duration in minutes (`duration`), start and end station names, 
rider type (`member_casual`), and `year` and `month`,
which I added based on the file names. The number of rides differs substantially 
across the four months, from 12,420 in January 2020 to 47,156 in July 2024. 
Ride duration ranges from `r round(min(citi_df$duration), 1)` 
to `r round(max(citi_df$duration), 1)` minutes, with a median 
of `r round(median(citi_df$duration), 1)` minutes, which is consistent with 
the 4-hour (240-minute) cutoff. 
About `r round(100 * mean(citi_df$rideable_type == "electric_bike"), 1)`% 
of rides used electric bikes. Missing values occur only in 
station names (`r sum(is.na(citi_df$start_station_name))` start stations 
and `r sum(is.na(citi_df$end_station_name))` end stations); 
all other variables are complete.



### Number of rides by year, month, and rider type
```{r}
citi_df |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(
    total = casual + member,
    pct_casual = round(100 * casual / total, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Number of rides by year, month, and rider type")

```
And from the table, we can infer that members account for the majority of rides 
in every month, but the share of casual riders varies strongly by season. 
In January, casual riders made up only 7.9% of rides in 2020 (984 of 12,420) 
and 11.2% in 2024 (2,108 of 18,861), whereas in July they made up 26.8% in 
2020 (5,637 of 21,048) and 23.1% in 2024 (10,894 of 47,156). 
Ridership also grew between 2020 and 2024, by about 52% in January and 124% in July. 
Casual rides in July nearly doubled (5,637 to 10,894), 
while member rides more than doubled (15,411 to 36,262), 
so the casual share in July declined slightly. 
These counts come from a 1% sample of rides, 
so they should be read as relative patterns rather than the true number of rides.




### Top 5 start stations, July 2024
```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |>
  count(start_station_name, name = "n_rides") |>
  arrange(desc(n_rides)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Top 5 start stations, July 2024")
```
The five most popular starting stations in July 2024 were Pier 61 at 
Chelsea Piers (163 rides), University Pl & E 14 St (155), W 21 St & 6 Ave (152), 
West St & Chambers St (150), and W 31 St & 7 Ave (146). 
The counts are close to one another, and each station accounts for 
only about 0.3% of the 47,156 rides in July 2024, so no single station dominates. 
The next two stations, Broadway & E 21 St (142) and 10 Ave & W 14 St (141), 
are only a few rides behind the fifth, so there is no clear gap separating 
the top five from the rest. Because the data are a 1% sample, small differences 
in rank among these stations may not be meaningful.



### Median ride duration by weekday
```{r}
citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = year, group = year)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by day of week,\nmonth, and year",
    x = "Day of week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year"
  )

citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = weekdays, values_from = median_duration) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Median ride duration (minutes)")

```
Median ride duration varies more by month and year than by day of the week. 
In both years, rides are longer in July than in January 
(2020: 13.4–16.5 vs. 8.5–10.0 minutes; 2024: 9.0–10.9 vs. 7.4–8.1 minutes). 
Rides in 2020 are also longer than rides in 2024 on every day of the week, 
with a larger gap in July (about 4–6 minutes) than in January (0.7–2.6 minutes). 
Within a week, medians are generally highest on weekends, 
most clearly in July 2020 (16.5 minutes vs. 13.4–14.2 on weekdays); 
the exception is January 2024, when Sunday (7.4 minutes) is tied for the lowest. 
These patterns are descriptive only, and because the data are a 1% sample, 
differences of a few tenths of a minute may not be meaningful.



### Ride duration distribution in 2024
```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride duration by membership, bike type,\nand month (2024)",
    x = "Rider type",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike type"
  )

citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  group_by(month, member_casual, rideable_type) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    median_duration = median(duration),
    q1 = quantile(duration, 0.25),
    q3 = quantile(duration, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Ride duration summary, 2024 (minutes)")

```
Since the data is right-skewed, Claude suggests me 
to use coord_cartesian() to adjust abit on the plot.

Ride durations are strongly right-skewed in every group: 
most rides are short, but a long tail extends to nearly 4 hours 
(the y-axis is truncated at 60 minutes for readability, 
so longer rides are not shown but are included in all statistics). 
Casual riders take longer and more variable rides than members in both months; 
for example, in July the median ride is 15.6 minutes for casual riders 
on classic bikes versus 7.7 minutes for members on classic bikes. 
Month matters mainly for casual riders, 
whose median duration is 2.9–3.6 minutes longer in July than in 
January (classic: 15.6 vs. 12.7; electric: 12.9 vs. 9.3), 
compared with 0.4–1.6 minutes among members. Bike type also affects 
the two groups differently: casual riders on classic bikes ride longer 
than those on electric bikes (15.6 vs. 12.9 minutes in July), 
whereas members on electric bikes ride slightly longer than those 
on classic bikes (9.2 vs. 7.7 minutes in July). The sample of casual 
classic-bike rides in January is small (n = 456), so that median is less stable. 
These are descriptive comparisons from a 1% sample and do not show 
why the groups differ.


I used Claude to help with troubleshooting, revising code, 
and checking my work against the style rubric. I reviewed and verified 
all code and interpretations myself.
